problemAnchor: 本节课的核心概念（SubstitutionEffect、IncomeEffect、LawOfDemand、LawOfSupply）之间有什么联系？学生在理解上最容易卡在哪里？

objective: The substitution effect: when the price of a good rises, consumers switch to substitute goods, reducing demand for the original good.；The income effect: when the price of a good rises, the consumer's purchasing power falls, reducing the quantity demanded of that good.；Law of demand: inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded; demand curve slopes downward.

learningGoals.statement: Distinguish between substitution effect and income effect and explain how each contributes to the law of demand.
State the law of demand and law of supply and identify the slope of each curve.
Determine market equilibrium and explain how prices adjust to eliminate surpluses and shortages.
Differentiate between a shift of a supply or demand curve and a movement along the curve.
Analyze the effects of changes in non-price factors on equilibrium price and quantity.

knowledgeNodes.name: SubstitutionEffect
knowledgeNodes.definition: When the price of a good rises, consumers substitute it with cheaper alternatives, reducing the quantity demanded of the original good.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.

knowledgeNodes.name: IncomeEffect
knowledgeNodes.definition: When the price of a good rises, the consumer's real income (purchasing power) falls, leading to a decrease in quantity demanded of that good.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.

knowledgeNodes.name: LawOfDemand
knowledgeNodes.definition: There is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus; demand curve slopes downward.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.

knowledgeNodes.name: LawOfSupply
knowledgeNodes.definition: There is a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied, ceteris paribus; supply curve slopes upward.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.

knowledgeNodes.name: MarketEquilibrium
knowledgeNodes.definition: The intersection of supply and demand curves, where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded; determines equilibrium price and quantity.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.

knowledgeNodes.name: ExcessSupplyDemand
knowledgeNodes.definition: Excess supply (surplus) when price > equilibrium, leading to downward price pressure; excess demand (shortage) when price < equilibrium, leading to upward price pressure.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.

knowledgeNodes.name: CurveShifts
knowledgeNodes.nameEn: Shifts in Supply and Demand Curves
knowledgeNodes.definition: Curve shifts are caused by factors other than the good's own price (e.g., technology, input costs, consumer tastes, government policies); they change equilibrium price and quantity.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Explain how various factors, including taxation, affect supply and demand.

knowledgeNodes.name: PriceSensitivity
knowledgeNodes.definition: The degree to which quantity demanded or supplied responds to price changes; influences the impact of curve shifts on equilibrium.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between the substitution effect and the income effect. Use an example of a price increase for a good.
questions.successCriteria: Student clearly distinguishes the two effects with appropriate terminology and example.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
questions.alignmentNote: Assesses deeper understanding of consumer behavior underlying demand.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can articulate the conceptual difference and apply it to a specific scenario.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may conflate the two effects or think they are the same.
questions.rubric: A strong answer should: (1) define substitution effect as switching to substitutes because the good becomes relatively more expensive; (2) define income effect as the reduction in real income reducing quantity demanded; (3) use a consistent example (e.g., coffee price rise leads to buying tea (substitution) and also buying less coffee overall due to feeling poorer (income effect)).
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: The substitution effect occurs when a price increase makes a good relatively more expensive, so consumers switch to alternatives (e.g., if coffee price rises, people buy more tea). The income effect occurs because the price rise reduces consumers' real income, so they buy less of the good (e.g., they also buy less coffee because they feel poorer). Both effects together cause quantity demanded to fall along a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.stem: Suppose the price of a good is currently above the equilibrium price. Describe what will happen in the market and how the price will adjust.
questions.successCriteria: Student describes surplus and the process of price falling to equilibrium.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
questions.alignmentNote: Assesses ability to apply equilibrium adjustment mechanism.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can predict market outcome when price is above equilibrium.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think above-equilibrium price leads to shortage or that price does not adjust.
questions.rubric: A strong answer should: (1) identify excess supply (surplus) because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded; (2) explain that sellers will lower the price to attract buyers; (3) describe that the price falls until it reaches equilibrium, where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: If the price is above equilibrium, there is a surplus: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. To sell their excess inventory, firms will lower the price. As the price falls, quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls until the market reaches equilibrium price, where supply equals demand.

questions.stem: Identify whether each of the following causes a shift in the supply curve or a movement along the supply curve: a) a rise in the wage paid to workers; b) a fall in the market price of the good.
questions.successCriteria: Student correctly classifies each as shift (wage rise) and movement (price fall) and explains why.
questions.ossdExpectation: Explain how various factors, including taxation, affect supply and demand.
questions.alignmentNote: Directly assesses ability to distinguish shift factors from price changes.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can apply the distinction between shift and movement to supply side.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think any change in price or cost causes a movement along the curve, conflating shift factors with own-price changes.
questions.rubric: A strong answer should: (a) identify wage rise as a shift – increased production costs reduce supply at every price, shifting the supply curve left; (b) identify a fall in market price as a movement along the supply curve – it changes the quantity supplied, not the supply itself; (c) explain that own-price changes cause movement, while external factors shift the curve.
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: a) A rise in wages increases production costs, so firms supply less at every price. This shifts the supply curve to the left (a decrease in supply). b) A fall in the market price of the good reduces the quantity supplied, but it is a movement along the existing supply curve (a decrease in quantity supplied), not a shift. The supply curve itself remains unchanged.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly identifies substitution effect as income effect or vice versa.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students confuse the substitution effect and income effect, thinking they are the same or swapping their definitions.

miniLesson.explain: When the price of a good rises, two effects reduce the quantity demanded. The substitution effect: consumers switch to substitute goods because the original good is now relatively more expensive. The income effect: the price rise reduces consumers' real income (purchasing power), so they buy less of the good. Both effects together cause the demand curve to slope downward.
miniLesson.example: Suppose the price of coffee rises. The substitution effect leads consumers to buy tea instead (a substitute). Simultaneously, the income effect means consumers feel poorer, so they buy less coffee overall. Both effects explain why quantity demanded falls.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Substitution = Switch to substitutes; Income = Income feels smaller.

guidedPractice.prompt: When the price of a good rises and consumers buy more of a substitute good, which effect is at work?
Explain how both the substitution effect and the income effect contribute to the law of demand when the price of a good increases. Use an example.
guidedPractice.answer: When the price of a good increases, the substitution effect causes consumers to switch to cheaper alternatives (e.g., buying tea instead of coffee), and the income effect reduces consumers' real income, leading them to buy less of the good. Both effects together decrease the quantity demanded, illustrating the inverse relationship of the law of demand.

guidedPractice.prompt: Analyze the following scenario: The price of gasoline rises sharply. Identify and distinguish the substitution effect and income effect on consumer behavior.
guidedPractice.answer: Substitution effect: Consumers may switch to public transit, carpooling, or more fuel-efficient cars to avoid paying higher gasoline prices. Income effect: The higher gasoline prices reduce consumers' real income, forcing them to cut back on overall driving and possibly other purchases. The substitution effect focuses on replacing gasoline with alternatives, while the income effect focuses on the reduction in purchasing power.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly states that price and quantity demanded move in the same direction on diagnostic question.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may mistakenly think the demand curve slopes upward (positive relationship between price and quantity demanded).

miniLesson.explain: The law of demand states an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: as price rises, quantity demanded falls; as price falls, quantity demanded rises. This is why the demand curve slopes downward from left to right. Two key reasons are the substitution effect (consumers switch to substitutes when price rises) and the income effect (higher price reduces purchasing power, so consumers buy less). Together, these effects ensure that higher prices lead to lower quantity demanded.
miniLesson.example: Consider strawberries. If the price of strawberries rises, consumers may buy more apples (substitution effect) and also feel poorer (income effect), so they buy fewer strawberries overall. Thus, the quantity demanded decreases as price increases.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Downhill Demand: as price climbs up, quantity demanded slides down.

guidedPractice.prompt: According to the law of demand, if the price of a good increases, what happens to the quantity demanded?
Explain two reasons why the demand curve slopes downward, using the concepts of substitution effect and income effect.
guidedPractice.answer: The substitution effect: when the price of a good rises, consumers switch to substitute goods, reducing demand for the original good. The income effect: when the price rises, the consumer's purchasing power falls, reducing the quantity demanded. Both effects cause quantity demanded to fall as price rises, creating a downward-sloping demand curve.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student argues that the demand curve for gasoline slopes upward because when price rises, people still need to drive. Explain why this reasoning is incorrect, using the law of demand and the substitution/income effects.
guidedPractice.answer: The student's reasoning is flawed because the law of demand still holds even for necessities. While gasoline has few close substitutes, higher prices still reduce quantity demanded through the income effect (higher gas prices reduce real income, so people may drive less or combine trips) and some substitution (e.g., using public transit). In the long run, consumers may buy more fuel-efficient cars. The demand curve for gasoline still slopes downward, though it may be steeper (more inelastic) than for goods with many substitutes.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly thinks supply curve slopes downward.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes that as price increases, quantity supplied decreases, possibly confusing supply with demand or misunderstanding producer incentives.

miniLesson.explain: The law of supply states that, ceteris paribus, there is a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied. When the price of a good rises, producers are willing to supply more of it because they can earn higher revenue. This is why the supply curve slopes upward from left to right. In contrast, a downward-sloping curve would imply that producers supply less when price increases, which contradicts profit-seeking behavior.
miniLesson.example: Consider the market for gasoline. If the price of gasoline rises, oil companies have an incentive to drill more and refine more gasoline to sell at the higher price. So the quantity supplied increases. Similarly, if the price falls, they reduce production. This positive relationship is the law of supply.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of 'S' in Supply as 'Same direction' – as Price goes Up, Quantity Supplied goes Up. The supply curve slopes Upward. Remember: More money, more product.

guidedPractice.prompt: According to the law of supply, when the price of a good increases, the quantity supplied typically: A) increases, B) decreases, C) stays the same, D) fluctuates randomly.
A farmer sells wheat. If the market price of wheat rises from $5 per bushel to $8 per bushel, what is the likely change in the quantity of wheat the farmer supplies? Explain briefly.
guidedPractice.answer: The farmer will likely increase the quantity supplied because the higher price makes it more profitable to grow and sell wheat. According to the law of supply, quantity supplied moves in the same direction as price.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student argues that supply curves should slope downward because as price rises, buyers buy less, so producers will produce less. Identify the mistake in this reasoning and correct it.
guidedPractice.answer: The student confuses the law of demand (buyer behavior) with the law of supply (producer behavior). While buyers reduce quantity demanded when price rises, producers respond to higher prices by increasing quantity supplied to maximize profit. The supply curve slopes upward, not downward. The law of supply focuses on seller incentives, not buyer reactions.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on question targeting this errorId
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think that prices are set by sellers rather than determined by supply and demand interaction.

miniLesson.explain: Market equilibrium price is determined by the intersection of supply and demand curves. Neither sellers nor buyers alone set the price. When the market price is above equilibrium, there is excess supply (surplus), and sellers lower prices. When the market price is below equilibrium, there is excess demand (shortage), and buyers bid up prices. The price adjusts until quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
miniLesson.example: Consider the market for strawberries. If sellers set the price at $5 per pint when equilibrium is $3, a surplus occurs. Sellers reduce the price to $3, where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. Buyers alone cannot set a lower price because sellers would not supply enough. The equilibrium price emerges from the interaction of both sides.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: The price is the meeting point: supply and demand shake hands at equilibrium.

guidedPractice.prompt: In a free market, the equilibrium price is determined by: A) sellers only, B) buyers only, C) the intersection of supply and demand, D) government.
guidedPractice.answer: C) the intersection of supply and demand.

guidedPractice.prompt: If the market price is above the equilibrium price, what will happen? Describe the adjustment process.
guidedPractice.answer: There will be a surplus (excess supply). Sellers will lower the price to attract buyers, and the price will fall until it reaches equilibrium where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose there is a sudden increase in demand for electric cars. Without changing supply, how does the equilibrium price adjust? Explain the role of buyers and sellers in this adjustment.
guidedPractice.answer: The increase in demand shifts the demand curve to the right, creating a shortage at the original price. Buyers compete, bidding up the price. The higher price incentivizes sellers to supply more, and the market moves to a new equilibrium with higher price and quantity. Buyers and sellers together determine the new price.

reteachModules.trigger: A student consistently identifies changes in consumer preferences as causing movement along the demand curve rather than a shift.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students confuse a shift of the supply or demand curve (caused by non-price factors) with a movement along the curve (caused by a change in the good's own price).

miniLesson.explain: A movement along a demand or supply curve occurs only when the good's own price changes. It represents a change in quantity demanded or quantity supplied. A shift of the entire curve occurs when a factor other than price changes (e.g., technology, consumer preferences, input costs). A shift means at every price, a different quantity is demanded or supplied.
miniLesson.example: Consumer income increases: this shifts the demand curve for strawberries to the right (shift). In contrast, if the price of strawberries falls, consumers move down along the existing demand curve to a higher quantity demanded (movement).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Price change moves you along; other factors shift the whole song.

guidedPractice.prompt: When the price of a good increases, what happens to the quantity demanded? Is this a shift of the demand curve or a movement along it?
A new technology reduces production costs for smartphones. Does this shift the supply curve or cause a movement along it? Why?
guidedPractice.answer: Shift (to the right). Because production cost is a non-price factor; at every price, firms are willing to supply more.

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose the government imposes a tax on gasoline, shifting the supply curve left. The resulting higher price causes consumers to buy less gasoline. Identify which change is a shift and which is a movement, and explain the sequence.
guidedPractice.answer: The tax shifts the supply curve left (a decrease in supply). The higher price then causes a movement along the demand curve to a lower quantity demanded (a decrease in quantity demanded).

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly identifies surplus when price is below equilibrium or shortage when price is above equilibrium.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often reverse the conditions: they think a price above equilibrium leads to a shortage and a price below leads to a surplus. Actually, above equilibrium causes a surplus, below causes a shortage.

miniLesson.explain: Excess supply (surplus) occurs when the market price is above the equilibrium price. At this price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, causing a surplus. Sellers respond by lowering prices to attract buyers, moving the market toward equilibrium. Excess demand (shortage) occurs when the market price is below equilibrium. Here, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage. Buyers bid up the price, moving the market toward equilibrium.
miniLesson.example: Imagine a market for strawberries. If the price is set at $5 per basket, but the equilibrium is $4, then at $5, farmers supply more than consumers want. That's a surplus. If the price is $3, consumers demand more than farmers supply, creating a shortage.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of a 'surplus' as 'too much' — price is too high, so there's a surplus. A 'shortage' is 'not enough' — price is too low, so there's a shortage. Above = surplus, below = shortage.

guidedPractice.prompt: If the market price is above equilibrium, is there a surplus or a shortage?
The current price of a good is $10, but the equilibrium price is $8. What is the market condition, and what is likely to happen to the price?
guidedPractice.answer: There is a surplus because price is above equilibrium. Sellers will lower the price toward $8.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why a price ceiling set below equilibrium leads to a shortage.
guidedPractice.answer: A price ceiling below equilibrium makes the price lower than the market-clearing price. At that low price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a persistent shortage because the price is not allowed to rise to equilibrium.

questions.stem: A consumer notices that the price of butter has increased and decides to buy margarine instead. Which effect does this behavior illustrate?

Imagine the price of movie tickets increases. Describe how the substitution effect and the income effect each reduce the quantity of movie tickets demanded. Use an example of a substitute good and explain the impact on real income.
questions.rubric: Student correctly identifies substitution effect (e.g., switch to streaming services or cheaper entertainment) and income effect (e.g., reduced purchasing power leads to fewer ticket purchases). Must clearly distinguish the two mechanisms.

retestCards.passRule: Answer the multiple-choice question correctly AND provide a clear explanation distinguishing both effects in the open-ended response (score at least 2/3 points).

questions.stem: According to the law of demand, if the price of a good increases, what happens to the quantity demanded?
Explain two economic reasons why the demand curve slopes downward. In your answer, define and apply the substitution effect and the income effect.
questions.rubric: Student correctly identifies substitution effect (consumers switch to substitutes when price rises) and income effect (higher price reduces purchasing power, leading to lower quantity demanded). Both effects must be explained and linked to the downward slope.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct answer for the multiple choice question and provide an explanation that includes both the substitution effect and the income effect, correctly describing how each contributes to the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

questions.stem: According to the law of supply, the supply curve typically slopes:

A friend tells you, 'When the price of a good goes up, producers will supply less because fewer people want to buy it.' Explain why your friend's statement is incorrect, and describe the correct relationship between price and quantity supplied.
questions.rubric: Response must identify that the friend confuses demand with supply. Correct explanation: The law of supply states a positive relationship – as price increases, quantity supplied increases because producers seek higher profits. Example or clear reasoning expected.

retestCards.passRule: Answer Q1 correctly (option A) and provide a Q2 response that correctly states that quantity supplied rises when price rises, and explains the mistake (confusing demand and supply or ignoring producer incentives).

questions.stem: In a free market, the equilibrium price is primarily determined by:
options: The intersection of supply and demand

questions.stem: Suppose the market price for a good is currently above the equilibrium price. Describe the adjustment process that will occur. In your answer, explain who (buyers, sellers, or both) is responsible for pushing the price toward equilibrium.
questions.rubric: Student must mention: (1) surplus/excess supply occurs because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded; (2) sellers lower the price to attract buyers; (3) the price continues to fall until it reaches equilibrium where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded; (4) both buyers and sellers interact to adjust price (buyers respond to lower prices, sellers actively lower price).

retestCards.passRule: Answer all questions correctly. For the open-ended question, the response must cover all points in the rubric.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a shift of the demand curve?
options: A decrease in the price of coffee leads to an increase in the quantity of coffee demanded.
An increase in consumer income leads to an increase in the demand for coffee at every price.
An increase in the price of coffee leads to a decrease in the quantity of coffee demanded.
A decrease in the price of tea leads to a decrease in the quantity of coffee demanded.

questions.stem: Suppose the government imposes a new tax on gasoline, shifting the supply curve left. The resulting higher price causes consumers to buy less gasoline. In your own words, explain which change is a shift of a curve and which is a movement along a curve, and why.
questions.rubric: Student must identify that the tax causes a shift of the supply curve (leftward) because it is a non-price factor. Then explain that the higher price causes a movement along the demand curve (to a lower quantity demanded) because it is a change in the good's own price.

retestCards.passRule: Answer both questions correctly. For open-ended, response must clearly distinguish shift from movement and correctly apply to the scenario.

questions.stem: In a market for gasoline, the equilibrium price is $1.50 per litre. If the current market price is $2.00 per litre, which of the following describes the market condition?
options: Excess demand (shortage), because price is above equilibrium.
Excess supply (surplus), because price is above equilibrium.
Excess demand (shortage), because price is below equilibrium.
Excess supply (surplus), because price is below equilibrium.

questions.stem: Suppose the equilibrium price for concert tickets is $100, but tickets are being sold on the secondary market for $80. Describe the market condition (surplus or shortage) and explain what will likely happen to the price as the market adjusts.
questions.rubric: Correctly identifies shortage (excess demand) because price is below equilibrium. Explains that buyers will bid up the price toward equilibrium. Accept mentions of higher demand than supply at that price.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly: Q1 with correct option, Q2 with identification of shortage and adjustment upward.

cards.question: A consumer buys fewer bus trips when the price of bus travel rises because they now have less purchasing power. This is an example of:
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can distinguish income effect from substitution effect in a real scenario.
misconceptions: The substitution effect involves switching to other goods, not a change in purchasing power.
✓ Correct. The price rise reduces real income, so the consumer buys fewer trips.
The law of demand states the overall relationship; this scenario illustrates a specific reason behind it.
While both effects operate, the scenario specifically describes reduced purchasing power, which is the income effect.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies income effect as the reason for decreased quantity demanded due to reduced real income.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
cards.alignmentNote: Assesses understanding of consumer response to price changes, part of supply/demand model.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think any change in quantity demanded due to price is the substitution effect, confusing it with income effect.

cards.question: When the price of coffee rises, a consumer buys more tea instead. This behavior is best explained by the:
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can identify substitution effect when a price increase leads to a switch to alternatives.
misconceptions: The income effect would focus on reduced purchasing power, not switching to a substitute.
✓ Correct. The consumer replaces coffee with tea, a substitute.
This is about consumer behavior, not producer behavior.
Excess demand refers to a shortage at below-equilibrium price, not a response to a price change.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies substitution effect as the consumer switching to a substitute good.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly assesses understanding of consumer substitution behavior.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think it's the income effect because the consumer is buying less coffee overall.

cards.question: According to the law of demand, if the price of a good increases, the quantity demanded:
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows the direction of the law of demand.
misconceptions: The law of demand states an inverse relationship; quantity demanded decreases when price rises.
✓ Correct. As price rises, quantity demanded falls.
Quantity demanded typically changes with price, ceteris paribus.
The law of demand predicts a clear inverse relationship.
cards.successCriteria: Student recalls inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly assesses knowledge of the law of demand.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think price and quantity demanded move together (positive relationship).

cards.question: The law of supply states that when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied typically:
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows the direction of the law of supply.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. Higher price incentivizes producers to supply more.
The law of supply says quantity supplied and price move in the same direction.
Quantity supplied typically responds positively to price changes.
The law of supply states a straightforward positive relationship.
cards.successCriteria: Student recalls positive relationship between price and quantity supplied.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly assesses knowledge of the law of supply.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think supply curves slope downward or that quantity supplied falls when price rises.

cards.question: In a free market, the equilibrium price is determined by:
options: The intersection of supply and demand
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows that equilibrium price arises from the interaction of both sides of the market.
misconceptions: Sellers can only ask a price; the market determines the equilibrium through supply and demand.
Buyers alone do not set the price; it is the interaction of supply and demand.
✓ Correct. Equilibrium price balances quantity supplied and quantity demanded.
In a free market, price is not set by government; it results from market forces.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies equilibrium as the intersection of supply and demand.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
cards.alignmentNote: Directly assesses understanding of market equilibrium.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think sellers alone set the price or that it is arbitrary.

cards.question: An increase in consumers' preference for a good causes the demand curve to:
cards.diagnosis: Check if student distinguishes between a shift (change in preference) and a movement along the curve (price change).
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. Increased preference raises demand at every price, shifting the curve right.
A positive change in preference increases demand, not decreases it.
Movement along the curve occurs only when the good's own price changes, not preferences.
Movement along the curve occurs only when the good's own price changes, not preferences.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that a change in taste shifts the demand curve.
cards.ossdExpectation: Explain how various factors, including taxation, affect supply and demand.
cards.alignmentNote: Assesses understanding of factors that shift demand, part of SE BB2.2.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think increased preference leads to a movement along the curve or causes a shift in the opposite direction.

cards.question: If the market price is below the equilibrium price, there will be a:
cards.diagnosis: Check if student remembers which price relative to equilibrium causes shortage or surplus.
misconceptions: A surplus occurs when price is above equilibrium, not below.
✓ Correct. At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage.
Equilibrium only occurs at the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
A price below equilibrium will lead to pressure for the price to rise.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that a price below equilibrium leads to excess demand (shortage).
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of models of supply and demand, including price elasticity, and apply these models to analyse selected economic decisions.
cards.alignmentNote: Assesses understanding of surplus and shortage conditions.

cards.question: Identify whether each of the following causes a shift in the supply curve or a movement along the supply curve: a) a rise in the wage paid to workers; b) a fall in the market price of the good.
